processing: An unoxidised green tea made from single early-spring buds and shaped flat and straight, under county production rules for the appellation.
harvest_season: Early spring; the buds of the first flush are the material the appellation is built on.
appearance_dry: Flat, straight, even buds with a moist green colour.
taste_profile: A persistent chestnut aroma over a fresh, mellow, sweet cup that holds up to several steeps.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for a flat bud green: a glass or gaiwan, water well off the boil, and no lid left on between steeps.

vintage_note: Like other Sichuan early-spring greens, it is meant to be bought from the current year's harvest and drunk within about a year. The local standard divides it into four grades, and the earliest bud lots normally sit at the top.
description:
Fuli tea is the green tea of Xiaohe town in Weiyuan county, in the Neijiang area of Sichuan. It is little known outside the province, but it has its own protected name, and the area is tightly drawn: fifteen villages plus a handful of tea farms.

The gardens sit in steep, wooded hill country crossed by the Yuexi River, on mildly acidic soils. The tea is made from single early-spring buds, using improved cultivars such as Fuding Dabai and Mingshan 131, and pressed into the flat, straight shape familiar from many Sichuan bud greens.

The character to look for is chestnut: a warm, lasting aroma, then a fresh and mellow cup with some sweetness. It is described as standing up well to repeat steeping. As with other flat bud greens, too-hot water is the common mistake, since it flattens the sweetness and brings out bitterness.

Buying it means looking for the current spring's harvest and, ideally, the grade. If you enjoy chestnut-toned greens, it is an interesting local comparison with better-known Sichuan teas such as Zhu Ye Qing.
history:
Local tradition holds that tea was already produced here in the Chunyou years of the Southern Song, but that is a legend rather than a documented start. Local accounts also link the area with the late Qing scholar Zhao Xi, who is said to have written an inscription for the Fuli tea trees while passing through Fuli market, now Xiaohe town, with students.

The firmer record is modern. Weiyuan county set out production and processing rules in 2008, and on 15 November 2010 the Ministry of Agriculture registered Fuli tea as a protected agricultural geographical indication.
